en.title: Aerospace Engineering: the whole course
en.short: What aerospace engineering covers, how degrees are organised, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What aerospace engineering is
sections.text: Aerospace engineering is the engineering of vehicles that travel through the atmosphere or in space. Aeronautics covers aircraft, helicopters and other atmospheric vehicles. Astronautics covers rockets, satellites and spacecraft. The work combines aerodynamics, structures, propulsion, materials, control, avionics and systems engineering. It also includes testing, maintenance, safety and regulation. The subject matters because these vehicles carry people and expensive equipment, and failure can be catastrophic. These summaries teach principles. They do not replace design codes, manufacturers’ manuals, test data or a qualified engineer. Airworthiness rules, design standards and registration differ by country. In Nigeria, engineering regulation is through COREN, the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria. Check the current official source for your country.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text: Aerospace degrees are organised differently by country and institution, so check your own handbook for length, awards and accreditation. In Nigeria, an engineering bachelor’s degree is commonly five years and includes industrial training under SIWES, the Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme. Polytechnic engineering routes usually use ND and HND awards, but aerospace-specific programmes vary. In the UK, a BEng commonly takes three years and an MEng four in England, Wales and Northern Ireland; Scottish degrees often take one year longer. In the United States, a bachelor’s degree commonly takes four years and programmes may be accredited by ABET. Early years are usually shared with other engineering students: mathematics, mechanics, thermodynamics, fluids, materials, drawing and computing. Later years add aerospace core subjects, laboratories, design projects and a final-year project. A master’s adds advanced analysis and a research dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
The introduction stage builds the tools. You start with what aerospace engineering is, then engineering mathematics, statics, dynamics and vibration, thermodynamics, fluid mechanics, materials, engineering drawing and CAD, and computing and numerical methods. These subjects are shared with other engineering students and are the base for later work.

The core stage applies those tools to flight vehicles. Incompressible aerodynamics and aerofoil theory come first, then compressible flow and gas dynamics. Aircraft performance and flight mechanics, stability and control explain how an aircraft flies and how it is controlled. Aircraft structures and aerospace materials selection and manufacturing deal with strength, stiffness and production. Propulsion splits into air-breathing engines and rocket propulsion. Orbital mechanics introduces space trajectories. Avionics and control systems and aircraft systems cover the electronic and mechanical systems on board. The aircraft design project brings these subjects together. Space systems engineering, wind tunnel and flight testing, computational methods such as CFD and finite elements, airworthiness, maintenance and aviation safety, and professional practice, ethics and regulation complete the core.

At master’s level, students study advanced aerodynamics and CFD, aeroelasticity and composite structures, advanced spacecraft dynamics and control, and research methods.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study by solving problems, not by reading only. For each topic, learn the assumptions behind the main equations and the units they use. Draw a diagram before calculating: a free-body diagram for statics, a control volume for fluids and thermodynamics, a free-body and coordinate system for flight mechanics, and an orbit sketch for orbital mechanics. Write units on every line and check whether the answer is reasonable. A wing span of 30 m and a lift of 10 N cannot both be right for a passenger aircraft.

Use software after you can do a simple hand calculation. Check CFD, finite element and simulation output against a known case or an approximate formula. Read accident reports and airworthiness material to connect theory with practice. Work in study groups for design projects, but keep your own calculations. Ask which codes and calculators are permitted.

sections.heading: Common mistakes students make

keyPoints: Aerospace engineering covers aircraft, helicopters, rockets, satellites and spacecraft, and the systems that support them.
These summaries teach principles and do not replace design codes, manuals, test data or a qualified engineer.
Degree length, awards and accreditation differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
In Nigeria, engineering regulation is through COREN, and industrial training commonly falls under SIWES.
Solve problems by hand, draw diagrams, write units and check that answers are reasonable.
Common errors include mixing units, misusing formulas outside their assumptions and trusting software output without checks.

en.title: Introduction to aerospace engineering
en.short: Aircraft, spacecraft, the standard atmosphere, aircraft anatomy, safety and careers.

sections.heading: What it covers
sections.text: Aerospace engineering designs and analyses vehicles that travel through air or space. It includes fixed-wing aircraft, helicopters, launch vehicles and spacecraft. Aircraft stay in the atmosphere; launch vehicles and spacecraft also work outside it, where there is no air to breathe or to burn fuel with. The same core ideas, forces, materials, propulsion and control, apply in both cases, but launch vehicles must carry their own oxidiser, and spacecraft must survive vacuum and, on re-entry, heating.

sections.heading: Standard atmosphere
sections.text:
To compare aircraft fairly, engineers use the International Standard Atmosphere (ISA), a model of average conditions, not today’s weather. At sea level ISA gives T0 = 288.15 K (15 °C), p0 = 101 325 Pa and density ρ0 = 1.225 kg/m³. In the troposphere, up to about 11 km, temperature falls by 6.5 K per km. Pressure and density fall with altitude; density falls mainly because pressure falls.

Example at 5 km: T = 288.15 − 6.5 × 5 = 255.65 K. Pressure is about 54 kPa and density about 0.74 kg/m³, about 60% of the sea-level density. Lower density means less lift for a given speed, so runways and engines must be sized for it.

sections.heading: Anatomy and disciplines
sections.text: An aircraft has a fuselage (body), wings, empennage (tail), landing gear and one or more engines. The main design disciplines are aerodynamics (airflow and lift), structures (loads and strength), propulsion, flight mechanics and control (how it flies and is steered), avionics (electronic systems), aircraft systems, and materials and manufacturing. These groups work together; a change in wing shape affects lift, weight and stress.

sections.heading: Safety and careers
sections.text: Safety is designed in, not added later. Engineers use redundancy (backup systems), fail-safe structures and testing. Airworthiness means the vehicle meets the safety standards set by a national regulator for its intended use. Regulators differ by country: the FAA in the United States, EASA in Europe and the NCAA in Nigeria. In Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering practice. Careers include design, stress analysis, propulsion, avionics, testing, maintenance, airworthiness and space systems.

keyPoints: ISA sea level: T0 = 288.15 K, p0 = 101 325 Pa, ρ0 = 1.225 kg/m³.
In the ISA troposphere, T = T0 − Lh with L = 6.5 K/km; pressure and density fall with altitude.
At 5 km the ISA gives about 255.7 K, 54 kPa and 0.74 kg/m³.
Aerospace covers aircraft, helicopters, launch vehicles and spacecraft.
Main disciplines: aerodynamics, structures, propulsion, flight mechanics and control, avionics, systems, materials.
Airworthiness is regulated nationally; examples are FAA (US), EASA (Europe) and NCAA (Nigeria); COREN regulates engineering practice in Nigeria.

en.title: Engineering mathematics for aerospace
en.short: Calculus, vectors, matrices, ODEs, series, complex numbers and transform methods for aerospace.

sections.heading: Calculus and series
sections.text: Calculus studies change and accumulation. A derivative gives a rate, such as velocity from position; an integral gives a total, such as work from force. Vector calculus adds gradient, divergence and curl, which describe slopes, sources and rotation of fields in fluid mechanics. A sequence is an ordered list; a series is its sum. Taylor series approximate a smooth function near a point. Example: e^x ≈ 1 + x + x²/2. At x = 0.1 this gives 1.105, against 1.10517.

sections.heading: Vectors and matrices
sections.text: A vector has magnitude and direction. The dot product a·b = |a||b|cos θ measures alignment; the cross product a×b gives a perpendicular vector and measures turning effect or area. For a = (1,2,2), |a| = √(1²+2²+2²) = 3. A matrix represents a linear transformation. Matrix multiplication composes transformations; determinants give volume scaling; eigenvalues describe natural modes and stability. Linear algebra solves Ax = b and supports structural and control models.

sections.heading: Differential equations
sections.text: An ordinary differential equation (ODE) relates a function to its derivatives. First-order ODEs model cooling and decay. Second-order linear ODEs model vibration, such as m x'' + c x' + k x = F(t). The solution has a transient part from the characteristic roots and a forced part. Example: x'' + 4x = 0 has roots r = ±2i, so x = A cos 2t + B sin 2t. Initial conditions fix A and B.

sections.heading: Transforms and complex numbers
sections.text: A complex number z = x + iy has real part x and imaginary part y, with i² = −1. Its modulus is |z| = √(x²+y²); argument is the angle in the complex plane. Complex exponentials simplify oscillations. The Laplace transform turns an ODE in time into an algebraic equation in s, useful in control. The Fourier series writes a periodic signal as sines and cosines; the Fourier transform extends this to non-periodic signals. They analyse vibration, fluid waves and signals.

keyPoints: Derivatives give rates and integrals give totals; vector calculus uses gradient, divergence and curl.
Dot product: a·b = |a||b|cos θ; cross product gives a perpendicular vector.
A matrix equation Ax = b is solved by linear algebra; eigenvalues describe modes and stability.
A linear ODE such as x'' + 4x = 0 has oscillatory solutions x = A cos 2t + B sin 2t.
Complex numbers use i² = −1 and modulus |z| = √(x²+y²); Laplace transforms convert ODEs to algebra in s, while Fourier methods represent signals as sine and cosine components.

en.title: Statics: forces, moments and equilibrium
en.short: Forces, moments, free-body diagrams, equilibrium, trusses, frames, friction and area properties.

sections.heading: Forces and moments
sections.text:
A force is a push or pull with magnitude, direction and point of application, so it is a vector. A moment is a force’s turning effect: M = F × d, where d is the perpendicular distance to the line of action. A couple is two equal, opposite, parallel forces; its moment is F × d about every point.

A free-body diagram isolates one body, replaces supports by reactions and shows all external loads.

sections.heading: Equilibrium
sections.text:
For a particle, equilibrium means ΣF = 0: ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0 in two dimensions; all three components are zero in three dimensions. For a rigid body, ΣM = 0 about any point. A two-dimensional body has three independent equations; a three-dimensional body has six.

Example: a 4 m beam on simple supports carries 10 kN at 1 m from the left. Moments about the left support: R_B × 4 − 10 × 1 = 0, so R_B = 2.5 kN. ΣFy gives R_A = 7.5 kN. Check: 7.5 + 2.5 = 10 kN.

sections.heading: Trusses and frames
sections.text:
A truss is a framework of slender members joined at pin joints, loaded only at joints. Each member is a two-force member in axial tension or compression. The method of joints applies ΣF = 0 at each joint, starting where at most two unknowns remain. The method of sections cuts the truss and applies equilibrium to one part.

Frames and machines contain multi-force members, with forces applied at more than two points. Dismember them and draw a free-body diagram of each part.

sections.heading: Friction and areas
sections.text: Dry friction opposes sliding. Limiting static friction is Fmax = μN, where μ is the coefficient of friction and N the normal force; kinetic friction is usually lower. A centroid is the centre of area: x̄ = ∫x dA ÷ A. The second moment of area is I = ∫y² dA about an axis; the parallel-axis theorem gives I = I_centroid + A d². Design codes vary by country.

keyPoints: A moment is M = F × d, with d perpendicular to the force line of action; a couple has the same moment about every point.
A particle is in equilibrium when ΣF = 0; a rigid body also needs ΣM = 0.
In two dimensions a rigid body has three independent equilibrium equations; in three dimensions it has six.
The method of joints applies joint equilibrium; the method of sections uses equilibrium of a cut part.
Limiting static friction is Fmax = μN; kinetic friction is usually lower.
For an area, x̄ = ∫x dA ÷ A and I = ∫y² dA, with I = I_centroid + A d² by the parallel-axis theorem.

en.title: Dynamics and vibration of mechanical systems
en.short: Particle and rigid-body dynamics, energy and momentum methods, fixed-axis rotation, and damped SDOF vibration.

sections.heading: Particle motion
sections.text: Kinematics describes motion without forces: position, velocity and acceleration. For constant acceleration, v = u + at and s = ut + ½at². Kinetics uses Newton’s laws. The second law, ΣF = ma, applies to a particle; a rigid body also needs moments. A rigid body keeps its shape, so its motion is translation plus rotation. Draw a free-body diagram before writing equations.

sections.heading: Work, energy, momentum
sections.text: Work-energy methods use W = ΔKE, where work is force times displacement along the force and kinetic energy is ½mv². They suit problems where forces vary or time is unknown. Impulse-momentum uses ∫F dt = Δp, with p = mv. Impulse is the force acting over time. These methods are scalar or vector statements of Newton’s laws, not new laws. For a rigid body, include rotational kinetic energy and angular momentum.

sections.heading: Fixed-axis rotation
sections.text: For rotation about a fixed axis, angular velocity ω and angular acceleration α describe motion. The equations mirror linear ones: ω = ω₀ + αt and θ = ω₀t + ½αt². Torque τ causes angular acceleration: τ = Iα, where I is the moment of inertia about the axis. Angular momentum is L = Iω, and rotational kinetic energy is ½Iω². The parallel-axis theorem moves I between parallel axes.

sections.heading: Vibration
sections.text:
A single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) system has one coordinate, such as a mass on a spring. Free vibration has no external force; its natural angular frequency is ωn = √(k/m). Damping dissipates energy. The damping ratio is ζ = c ÷ (2√(km)); critical damping is c_c = 2√(km). For ζ < 1, damped frequency is ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²). Forced vibration is driven by an external force; resonance occurs when the forcing frequency is near ωn and amplitude peaks unless damping is large.

Example: m = 2 kg, k = 2000 N/m, c = 40 N·s/m. ωn = √(2000 ÷ 2) = 31.6 rad/s. ζ = 40 ÷ (2√(4000)) = 0.316. ωd = 31.6√(1 − 0.316²) = 30.0 rad/s.

keyPoints: Newton’s second law for a particle is ΣF = ma; for a rigid body use ΣF = ma at the centre of mass and ΣM = Iα about a fixed axis or the centre of mass.
Work-energy: W = ΔKE; impulse-momentum: ∫F dt = Δp.
For fixed-axis rotation, τ = Iα, L = Iω and rotational kinetic energy is ½Iω².
SDOF free vibration has natural frequency ωn = √(k/m).
Damping ratio ζ = c ÷ (2√(km)); for ζ < 1 the damped frequency is ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²).
Resonance occurs when the forcing frequency is near ωn; damping limits the amplitude.

en.title: Thermodynamics for aerospace
en.short: Laws of thermodynamics, properties, work, heat, entropy, and the Carnot and Brayton cycles.

sections.heading: Laws and properties
sections.text: Thermodynamics studies energy, heat and work. The zeroth law says that if two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they share a temperature. The first law is energy conservation: for a closed system, Q − W = ΔU, where Q is heat added, W is work done by the system and U is internal energy. A pure substance has phases and saturation properties, often read from tables. An ideal gas obeys pV = mRT, with cp − cv = R and γ = cp ÷ cv.

sections.heading: Work, heat, enthalpy
sections.text: Work is energy transferred by a force moving through a distance; boundary work is ∫p dV. Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Both are path-dependent, while U is a state property. Enthalpy is H = U + pV, or h = u + pv per unit mass. Steady-flow devices use enthalpy. Example: air with cp = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K) heated from 300 K to 500 K gains Δh = cpΔT = 1.005 × 200 = 201 kJ/kg.

sections.heading: Entropy and reversibility
sections.text: Entropy S measures energy dispersal and unavailable work. For a reversible path, dS = δQrev ÷ T. The second law says the entropy of an isolated system cannot decrease. Friction, mixing and finite temperature differences make real processes irreversible and create entropy. A reversible process is an ideal limit: quasi-static (slow enough to stay near equilibrium), with no friction or other losses. Carnot efficiency is η = 1 − Tc ÷ Th, using absolute temperatures.

sections.heading: Carnot and Brayton cycles
sections.text: The Carnot cycle has two reversible isothermal and two reversible adiabatic processes. It gives the highest efficiency possible between two reservoirs. The Brayton cycle models a gas turbine or jet engine: compression, constant-pressure heat addition, expansion and constant-pressure heat rejection. In the ideal air-standard form (working fluid treated as air), compression and expansion are isentropic. Its efficiency is η = 1 − 1 ÷ rp^((γ−1)÷γ), where rp is pressure ratio. Example: rp = 10 and γ = 1.4 give η = 1 − 1 ÷ 10^(0.2857) = 0.482, or 48.2%. Real engines are lower.

keyPoints: First law for a closed system: Q − W = ΔU.
Ideal gas: pV = mRT, cp − cv = R and γ = cp ÷ cv.
Enthalpy: h = u + pv; steady-flow devices use it.
Second law: entropy of an isolated system cannot decrease; dS = δQrev ÷ T for a reversible path.
Carnot efficiency: η = 1 − Tc ÷ Th, with absolute temperatures.
Ideal Brayton efficiency: η = 1 − 1 ÷ rp^((γ−1)÷γ).

en.title: Fluid mechanics: properties and flow fundamentals
en.short: Fluid properties, pressure, continuity, Bernoulli, momentum, viscosity and boundary layers.

sections.heading: Fluid properties and pressure
sections.text:
A fluid deforms continuously under shear stress. Density ρ is mass per volume; specific weight is ρg. Pressure p is normal force per area. In a static fluid, p = p0 + ρgh, where h is depth below the surface. Gauge pressure is above atmospheric; absolute pressure adds atmospheric pressure. A manometer measures pressure difference from a liquid column height.

Example: water at h = 10 m, ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²: p − p0 = ρgh = 1000 × 9.81 × 10 = 98,100 Pa, about 98.1 kPa.

sections.heading: Continuity and momentum
sections.text:
For steady flow, continuity conserves mass: ρ1A1V1 = ρ2A2V2. If the fluid is incompressible, A1V1 = A2V2, so a narrower pipe gives faster flow. Bernoulli’s equation applies along a streamline in steady, incompressible, inviscid flow: p + ½ρV² + ρgz = constant. The momentum equation for a control volume is ΣF = ρQ(Vout − Vin), in vector form; it gives forces on bends and vanes.

Example: A1 = 0.01 m², V1 = 2 m/s, A2 = 0.005 m². Then V2 = A1V1 ÷ A2 = 0.01 × 2 ÷ 0.005 = 4 m/s.

sections.heading: Viscosity and boundary layers
sections.text:
Viscosity resists shear. A Newtonian fluid has τ = μ du/dy, where μ is dynamic viscosity and du/dy is the velocity gradient. Kinematic viscosity is ν = μ/ρ.

Laminar flow moves in smooth layers; turbulent flow has eddies. The Reynolds number Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν indicates the regime, but the change depends on geometry, so check the accepted value for your case. A boundary layer is the thin region near a surface where viscous effects matter; it may be laminar or turbulent and can separate.

sections.heading: Dimensional analysis
sections.text:
Dimensional analysis groups variables into dimensionless numbers. The Buckingham Pi theorem says that n variables with m basic dimensions form n − m independent groups.

Models predict full-size behaviour when the relevant groups match; for pipe flow the key group is Re.

keyPoints: Static pressure rises with depth: p = p0 + ρgh.
Continuity for steady flow is ρ1A1V1 = ρ2A2V2; for incompressible flow A1V1 = A2V2.
Bernoulli along a streamline for steady, incompressible, inviscid flow: p + ½ρV² + ρgz = constant.
The steady momentum equation is ΣF = ρQ(Vout − Vin) in vector form.
A Newtonian fluid has τ = μ du/dy, and kinematic viscosity is ν = μ/ρ.
The Reynolds number Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν indicates the regime; a boundary layer is the thin viscous region near a surface, and dimensional analysis forms groups such as Re.

en.title: Materials for aerospace: structure and properties
en.short: Atomic structure, defects, tensile behaviour, hardness, impact, fatigue, creep and material classes.

sections.heading: Structure and defects
sections.text:
Atoms pack in regular patterns called crystals. Metals are crystalline with many grains, each a small crystal with its own orientation. Polymers are long chain molecules, often partly amorphous (not crystalline) and partly crystalline. Ceramics have strong ionic or covalent bonds. Composites combine phases, such as stiff fibres in a polymer matrix.

Defects matter. A vacancy is a missing atom. A dislocation is a line defect; its movement lets metals deform plastically. Grain boundaries block dislocations, so smaller grains strengthen metals.

sections.heading: Tensile test
sections.text:
The tensile test pulls a specimen and records force and extension. Engineering stress is σ = F ÷ A₀, where A₀ is the original area; engineering strain is ε = ΔL ÷ L₀. In the elastic region Hooke’s law applies: σ = Eε, where E is Young’s modulus.

Beyond yield, deformation is plastic and permanent. The highest stress is the ultimate tensile strength. Ductility is strain before fracture; toughness is energy absorbed.

Example: A₀ = 100 mm² and F = 20 kN give σ = 20,000 ÷ 100 = 200 N/mm². Extension 0.10 mm over 50 mm gives ε = 0.002. If elastic, E = 200 ÷ 0.002 = 100 GPa.

sections.heading: Hardness and time effects
sections.text: Hardness is resistance to indentation or scratching. Impact tests apply a sudden load and measure energy absorbed. Fatigue is damage under repeated stress; cracks start at defects and can grow below yield. Some steels show an endurance limit, a stress below which they do not fail by fatigue, but many materials do not. Creep is slow, permanent deformation under sustained load at high temperature.

sections.heading: Material classes
sections.text:
Metals are strong and ductile; structure and alloying control strength. Aluminium and titanium alloys are common in airframes, and nickel superalloys in hot engine parts.

Polymers are light and easy to shape but less stiff and strong. Ceramics are hard and heat resistant but brittle. Composites give high stiffness and strength per unit mass, but properties depend on fibre direction and interface. Structure at every scale sets properties.

keyPoints: Engineering stress is σ = F ÷ A₀ and engineering strain is ε = ΔL ÷ L₀.
In the elastic region σ = Eε; plastic deformation is permanent.
Dislocations allow plastic flow, and grain boundaries hinder it.
Fatigue is repeated-stress damage; creep is time-dependent deformation at high temperature.
Metals, polymers, ceramics and composites differ because their atomic and molecular structures differ.
Hardness measures indentation resistance, and impact tests measure energy absorbed under sudden load.

en.title: Engineering drawing and computer-aided design
en.short: Orthographic views, sections, dimensioning, limits and fits, surface finish and CAD models for manufacture.

sections.heading: Views and sections
sections.text: Orthographic projection represents a three-dimensional object by separate two-dimensional views, usually front, top and side, projected onto planes at right angles. First-angle and third-angle projection arrange the same views differently; the projection symbol on the drawing tells you which convention is used. A section view cuts away material along a cutting plane to show hidden internal features, and the cut surface is hatched. An auxiliary view is projected onto a plane parallel to an inclined face so that the face appears in true shape and size.

sections.heading: Dimensioning and fits
sections.text:
Dimensioning gives the size and location of features. Work from a datum, avoid duplicate dimensions, and add tolerances where variation matters. A tolerance is the allowed range between upper and lower limits. Fits describe how loose or tight a hole and shaft are: clearance, interference or transition. Limits-and-fits systems, such as ISO 286, define standard tolerances, but national and company practice varies.

Worked example: nominal 25 mm. Hole limits 25.000 mm and 25.021 mm; shaft limits 24.980 mm and 24.993 mm.
Maximum clearance = 25.021 − 24.980 = 0.041 mm.
Minimum clearance = 25.000 − 24.993 = 0.007 mm.
Both are positive, so this is a clearance fit.

sections.heading: Surface and assemblies
sections.text: Surface finish specifies how smooth a surface must be, often by roughness Ra in micrometres; the symbol and value follow the drawing standard in use. Standard parts such as bolts, bearings and keys are not redrawn in detail. They are called out by a standard designation and listed in the assembly drawing’s parts list or bill of materials. Assembly drawings show how parts fit together; exploded views help manufacture and maintenance.

sections.heading: CAD for manufacture
sections.text: CAD builds a parametric three-dimensional model from sketches, dimensions and constraints. From the model, associative two-dimensional drawings are generated with views, sections and dimensions; a model change updates the drawing. For manufacture, the drawing must be complete: state units, projection convention, tolerances, surface finish and revision. CAD formats and standards differ by country and employer, so follow the project’s stated standard.

keyPoints: Orthographic projection uses separate views at right angles; first-angle and third-angle arrange them differently, so check the projection symbol.
A section view shows internal features by cutting along a plane; an auxiliary view shows an inclined face in true shape.
Dimension from a datum and avoid duplicate dimensions; a tolerance is the allowed range between upper and lower limits.
For a hole and shaft, maximum clearance = hole maximum − shaft minimum and minimum clearance = hole minimum − shaft maximum.
Surface finish is specified by roughness such as Ra, and standard parts are called out by designation and listed in the bill of materials.
CAD models should drive associative drawings, and every manufacturing drawing needs units, projection, tolerances, surface finish and revision control stated.

en.title: Computing and numerical methods for aerospace
en.short: Programming, floating-point error, root finding, interpolation, integration and ODE methods.

sections.heading: Programs and algorithms
sections.text: Programming fundamentals are variables, conditionals, loops and functions. A variable names a stored value; a conditional chooses between branches; a loop repeats steps; a function packages a calculation. An algorithm is a finite, unambiguous sequence of steps that solves a problem. Pseudocode writes an algorithm in plain structure before coding it.

sections.heading: Floating point and error
sections.text: Floating-point representation stores a real number as sign, significand (the significant digits) and exponent in a fixed number of bits, so most values are rounded. Machine epsilon is the gap between 1 and the next representable number. Absolute error is |approximate − exact|; relative error is absolute error ÷ |exact|. Round-off error comes from finite precision; truncation error comes from replacing an infinite process by a finite one.

sections.heading: Roots and fitting
sections.text: Root finding solves f(x) = 0. Bisection brackets a sign change and halves the interval each step. Newton-Raphson uses x1 = x0 − f(x0) ÷ f′(x0). Interpolation passes a curve through known points; least-squares fitting finds a simple curve that need not pass through every point. Example: for f(x) = x² − 2 with x0 = 1, f = −1 and f′ = 2, so x1 = 1 − (−1) ÷ 2 = 1.5. Repeating gives 1.4167, close to √2.

sections.heading: Integration, derivatives, ODEs
sections.text: Numerical integration approximates the area under a curve. The trapezium rule is h/2 [f0 + 2f1 + ... + 2f(n−1) + fn], where h is the step. Numerical differentiation uses finite differences, for example f′(x) ≈ (f(x+h) − f(x−h)) ÷ (2h). For an ordinary differential equation (ODE) y′ = f(t, y), Euler’s method gives y(n+1) = y(n) + h f(t(n), y(n)); Runge-Kutta methods are more accurate.

keyPoints: An algorithm is a finite, unambiguous sequence of steps; programs use variables, conditionals, loops and functions.
Floating-point numbers are rounded, so test equality with a tolerance rather than exact comparison.
Absolute error = |approximate − exact|; relative error = absolute error ÷ |exact|.
Bisection needs a sign change; Newton-Raphson uses x1 = x0 − f(x0) ÷ f′(x0).
Trapezium rule: integral ≈ h/2 [f0 + 2f1 + ... + 2f(n−1) + fn].
Euler method: y(n+1) = y(n) + h f(t(n), y(n)); smaller h reduces truncation error but increases round-off.

en.title: Incompressible aerodynamics and aerofoil theory
en.short: Potential flow, circulation, Kutta condition, thin aerofoils, finite wings and high-lift devices.

sections.heading: Potential flow
sections.text: Incompressible potential flow assumes inviscid, irrotational flow. The velocity potential φ gives u = ∂φ/∂x and v = ∂φ/∂y, and satisfies Laplace’s equation. The stream function ψ gives u = ∂ψ/∂y and v = −∂ψ/∂x; ψ is constant along a streamline, and ψ₂ − ψ₁ is the volume flow per unit depth between two streamlines. Circulation Γ = ∮ V·ds measures rotation; for a potential vortex it is constant.

sections.heading: Lift and Kutta
sections.text: Circulation around an aerofoil generates lift. The Kutta-Joukowski theorem gives lift per unit span L' = ρUΓ, where ρ is density, U is free-stream speed and Γ is circulation. At a sharp trailing edge the Kutta condition requires flow to leave smoothly with finite velocity. It selects the circulation that places the rear stagnation point at the trailing edge. Real viscosity enforces this condition; without it, potential flow gives no unique lift.

sections.heading: Thin aerofoil
sections.text: Thin aerofoil theory treats a thin, slightly cambered section at small incidence. It gives cl = 2π(α − αL0), with α in radians; αL0 is the zero-lift angle set by camber. Pressure coefficient Cp = (p − p∞) ÷ (½ρU²) = 1 − (V ÷ U)², so faster upper-surface flow means lower pressure. Example: α = 6° = 0.1047 rad and αL0 = −2° = −0.0349 rad. Then α − αL0 = 0.1396 rad and cl = 2π × 0.1396 = 0.877.

sections.heading: Finite wings and high lift
sections.text: A finite wing has higher pressure below and lower pressure above, so air spills around the tips. Tip vortices create downwash, which tilts lift rearward and produces induced drag. For elliptic loading CDi = CL² ÷ (π AR), where AR = b² ÷ S; more generally CDi = CL² ÷ (π e AR), with span efficiency e ≤ 1. High-lift devices raise CL at low speed: flaps increase camber and sometimes area, while slats and leading-edge devices delay stall. They add drag and complexity.

keyPoints: Potential flow is inviscid and irrotational; φ satisfies Laplace’s equation and ψ is constant along a streamline.
Circulation is Γ = ∮ V·ds, and Kutta-Joukowski lift per unit span is L' = ρUΓ.
The Kutta condition fixes circulation by requiring smooth flow from a sharp trailing edge.
Thin aerofoil lift coefficient is cl = 2π(α − αL0), with α in radians.
Pressure coefficient is Cp = 1 − (V ÷ U)², so faster flow gives lower pressure.
Finite-wing induced drag is CDi = CL² ÷ (π e AR), with e ≤ 1; high-lift devices raise CL at low speed.

en.title: Compressible flow and gas dynamics
en.short: One-dimensional compressible flow: sound speed, Mach number, isentropic flow, nozzles, shocks and expansion fans.

sections.heading: Sound speed and Mach
sections.text:
One-dimensional compressible flow varies along the flow direction only. Sound speed is a = √(γRT), with γ the specific-heat ratio, R the gas constant and T absolute temperature. Mach number is M = V ÷ a. M < 1 is subsonic, M = 1 sonic and M > 1 supersonic.

Example: air at 300 K, γ = 1.4 and R = 287 J/(kg·K), gives a = √(1.4 × 287 × 300) = 347 m/s. At V = 200 m/s, M = 0.576.

sections.heading: Isentropic stagnation
sections.text:
Stagnation properties (subscript 0) are values reached if flow is brought to rest isentropically. For a constant-specific-heat ideal gas:
T0 ÷ T = 1 + (γ − 1) ÷ 2 × M²
p0 ÷ p = (T0 ÷ T)^(γ ÷ (γ − 1))
ρ0 ÷ ρ = (T0 ÷ T)^(1 ÷ (γ − 1))
These apply in isentropic regions, not across a shock. For the example, T0 = 300 × (1 + 0.2 × 0.576²) = 319.9 K.

sections.heading: Nozzles and choking
sections.text: In a converging nozzle the area falls to a throat. At a low enough back pressure M = 1 at the throat and the nozzle is choked: further reducing back pressure cannot increase mass flow. A converging-diverging nozzle has a throat then a diverging section. With a sonic throat and low enough back pressure, the diverging section accelerates flow to supersonic speed; otherwise it acts as a diffuser.

sections.heading: Shocks and expansions
sections.text: A normal shock is a change perpendicular to the flow. Ahead is supersonic, behind subsonic. It is not isentropic: total pressure falls and entropy rises, while total temperature stays constant. The pressure jump is p2 ÷ p1 = 1 + [2γ ÷ (γ + 1)] × (M1² − 1). An oblique shock is inclined to the flow; only the normal Mach component enters the jump relations, and the flow turns toward the shock. An expansion fan turns flow away and is isentropic, with Mach rising and pressure and temperature falling.

keyPoints: Sound speed is a = √(γRT) and Mach number is M = V ÷ a.
Stagnation relations: T0 ÷ T = 1 + (γ − 1) ÷ 2 × M² and p0 ÷ p = (T0 ÷ T)^(γ ÷ (γ − 1)).
A converging nozzle chokes when M = 1 at the throat; lowering back pressure further cannot raise mass flow.
A converging-diverging nozzle needs a sonic throat and low enough back pressure to give supersonic flow in the diverging section.
Across a normal shock flow becomes subsonic, total pressure falls and entropy rises; p2 ÷ p1 = 1 + [2γ ÷ (γ + 1)] × (M1² − 1).
Oblique shocks use the normal Mach component; expansion fans are isentropic and raise Mach number.

en.title: Aircraft performance
en.short: Standard atmosphere, drag polars, thrust and power, take-off, climb, cruise, range and load limits.

sections.heading: Atmosphere and polars
sections.text:
The International Standard Atmosphere (ISA) is a model for comparing performance. At sea level it gives 15 °C, 101 325 Pa and density 1.225 kg/m³; troposphere temperature falls about 6.5 K/km. Density falls with altitude, so lift and thrust fall unless speed rises.

Lift is L = ½ ρ V² S CL and drag D = ½ ρ V² S CD, where ρ is density, V true airspeed and S wing area. The drag polar is CD = CD0 + K CL², with K = 1 ÷ (π e AR), e Oswald efficiency and AR = b² ÷ S. Maximum L/D occurs when CD0 = K CL².

sections.heading: Thrust, power and climb
sections.text:
In steady level flight L = W and T = D, so thrust required TR = W ÷ (L/D). Power required PR = TR × V. Available thrust and power vary with speed and altitude.

Excess power gives climb: ROC = (PA − PR) ÷ W approximately, where ROC is rate of climb and PA power available. The ceiling is where excess power is zero.

Example: W = 50 kN, L/D = 15, V = 100 m/s. TR = 50 000 ÷ 15 = 3 333 N. PR = 3 333 × 100 = 333 300 W, about 333 kW.

sections.heading: Take-off, landing and cruise
sections.text:
Take-off and landing distances depend on weight, density altitude, wind, runway condition, braking and configuration. Certification rules set safety speeds and required distances; they differ by country and aircraft category, so use the flight manual and current national rules.

Cruise range and endurance depend on specific fuel consumption, speed, altitude and L/D. A payload-range diagram shows the trade-off between payload, fuel and range. Maximum endurance occurs near minimum fuel flow, not always at maximum-range speed.

sections.heading: Load factors and limits
sections.text: Load factor n = L ÷ W. In level flight n = 1; in a steady bank at angle φ, n = 1 ÷ cos φ. Manoeuvring and gust limits are set by certification requirements and vary with aircraft category and country. A V-n diagram plots speed against permissible load factor. Exceeding limits risks structural failure.

keyPoints: ISA sea-level values are 15 °C, 101 325 Pa and 1.225 kg/m³, with about 6.5 K/km lapse rate in the troposphere.
The drag polar is CD = CD0 + K CL², where K = 1 ÷ (π e AR).
In steady level flight L = W and T = D; thrust required is W ÷ (L/D), power required is TR × V, and rate of climb is about (PA − PR) ÷ W.
Range and endurance depend on fuel flow, speed and L/D; payload-range diagrams show the trade-off.
Load factor is n = L ÷ W, and in a steady bank n = 1 ÷ cos φ.
Take-off, landing and load limits come from national certification rules and the flight manual, so check the current official source.

en.title: Flight mechanics, stability and control
en.short: Six-degree-of-freedom motion, axes, stability derivatives, static and dynamic stability, controls and handling qualities.

sections.heading: Axes and equations
sections.text: Flight mechanics treats the aircraft as a rigid body with six degrees of freedom: three translations and three rotations. A common body axis set has x forward, y starboard and z down. Newton and Euler give m(dV/dt + ω × V) = F and I(dω/dt) + ω × (Iω) = M. Aerodynamic and propulsive terms make these equations nonlinear, and gravity couples them. Engineers linearise them about trim to study stability.

sections.heading: Derivatives and static stability
sections.text:
Stability derivatives are partial derivatives of force or moment coefficients with a state variable, such as Cmα = ∂Cm/∂α, at trim. Under the usual convention, static longitudinal stability needs Cmα < 0: a nose-up disturbance gives a nose-down moment. Static margin is often −Cmα ÷ CLα. Lateral-directional stability uses Clβ (dihedral effect) and Cnβ (weathercock stability); with the usual signs, Clβ < 0 and Cnβ > 0.

Example: Cm = Cm0 + Cmα α + Cmδe δe. With Cm0 = 0.02, Cmα = −0.8 per rad, Cmδe = −1.2 per rad and α = 0.05 rad, trim gives δe = −(0.02 − 0.04) ÷ (−1.2) = −0.0167 rad = −0.95°.

sections.heading: Dynamic modes and controls
sections.text: The linearised equations give the longitudinal short-period mode, a fast pitch and angle-of-attack oscillation, and the phugoid, a slow exchange of speed and height. Lateral-directional modes are roll subsidence, spiral mode and Dutch roll, a combined roll-yaw oscillation. Control surfaces create moments: elevator pitch, ailerons roll, rudder yaw. Effectiveness is moment per unit deflection, described by derivatives such as Cmδe; the moment scales with dynamic pressure q = ½ρV², so authority falls at low speed.

sections.heading: Handling qualities
sections.text: Handling qualities describe how easily a pilot performs tasks within the flight envelope. They are judged against flying qualities requirements and pilot rating scales such as Cooper-Harper. Requirements differ by country, authority and aircraft category, for example the US FAA, Europe’s EASA and Nigeria’s NCAA; check the current official source. Design codes and professional registration also differ by country, for example COREN in Nigeria.

keyPoints: Six-degree-of-freedom equations: m(dV/dt + ω × V) = F and I(dω/dt) + ω × (Iω) = M.
Stability derivatives are partial derivatives of coefficients at trim, such as Cmα = ∂Cm/∂α.
Static longitudinal stability requires Cmα < 0 under the usual convention; static margin is often −Cmα ÷ CLα.
Longitudinal dynamic modes are short-period and phugoid; lateral-directional modes are roll subsidence, spiral and Dutch roll.
Control effectiveness is moment per unit deflection and scales with q = ½ρV².
Handling qualities are assessed against national flying qualities requirements and pilot rating scales; check the current source.

en.title: Aircraft structures: semi-monocoque, shear flow and fatigue
en.short: Semi-monocoque design, shear flow, wing and fuselage bending, buckling, fatigue and design philosophies.

sections.heading: Semi-monocoque and thin walls
sections.text: A semi-monocoque structure uses skin, stringers, frames and longerons together. The skin carries shear and pressure; stringers and longerons carry bending; frames keep shape and support the skin. Cutouts need reinforcement because they interrupt load paths. Thin-walled sections are idealised as skins plus booms, lumped stringer areas that carry the direct stress. Open sections twist easily; closed sections are stiff in torsion.

sections.heading: Shear flow and torsion
sections.text: Wings and fuselages are thin-walled boxes and shells. Shear flow q is shear force per unit length along a thin wall. For a cut section, q = VQ ÷ I, with Q the first moment of area beyond the cut and I the second moment of area. In a closed cell q = qb + q0; q0 is found from zero twist. The shear centre is where a shear load causes no twist, not generally the centroid. Bending stress is σ = M y ÷ I. For a closed cell under torsion T, Bredt-Batho gives q = T ÷ (2A), where A is enclosed area, and τ = q ÷ t. Example: T = 10 kN·m, A = 0.2 m², t = 2 mm. q = 10,000 ÷ (2 × 0.2) = 25,000 N/m = 25 N/mm; τ = 25 ÷ 2 = 12.5 N/mm².

sections.heading: Buckling, fatigue and design
sections.text: Stiffened panels can buckle locally in the skin, as columns in the stiffeners, or as a whole panel. Design uses effective width (the skin width assumed to still carry load with a stiffener after local buckling), tests and code allowables. Fatigue is repeated stress causing cracks. Miner’s rule estimates damage: D = Σ(ni ÷ Ni), where ni is cycles at a stress level and Ni is life at that level; failure is predicted when D reaches 1. Safe-life retires a part after a fixed life. Fail-safe provides redundant load paths so a crack or failed member does not cause loss of the aircraft. Damage-tolerant design allows cracks, predicts growth, and sets inspection intervals. Certification rules differ by country; check the official rule.

keyPoints: Semi-monocoque skin, stringers, frames and longerons share load; cutouts need reinforcement.
Shear flow in a cut thin wall is q = VQ ÷ I; closed cells add a constant q0.
The shear centre is the load point causing no twist, not generally the centroid.
Bending stress is σ = M y ÷ I; closed-cell torsion gives q = T ÷ (2A) and τ = q ÷ t.
Stiffened panels can buckle locally, as stiffener columns or as a whole panel; allowables come from tests and codes.
Fatigue damage can be estimated by Miner’s rule D = Σ(ni ÷ Ni); safe-life, fail-safe and damage-tolerant design use different retirement and inspection rules.

en.title: Aerospace materials selection and manufacturing
en.short: Choosing airframe and engine materials, composite lay-up, joining, NDT and quality control.

sections.heading: Selection drivers
sections.text: Material choice balances specific strength and stiffness (each divided by density), fatigue and corrosion resistance, temperature capability, cost and manufacturability. Aluminium alloys are common in airframes because they are light, stiff and cheap, but they lose strength at moderate temperatures. Titanium alloys such as Ti-6Al-4V suit hot airframe parts and some engine components. Steels give high strength for landing gear and fasteners. Nickel superalloys keep strength at high temperature in engine hot sections. Composites offer high specific strength and stiffness and can be tailored, but are sensitive to impact, moisture and temperature.

sections.heading: Composite laminates
sections.text: A composite is a fibre reinforcement in a matrix. A lamina is one ply; a laminate is stacked plies. Fibres give high stiffness along their direction. The rule of mixtures estimates the longitudinal modulus E1 = VfEf + VmEm, where V is volume fraction. Example: Vf = 0.6, Ef = 230 GPa, Em = 3.5 GPa, so E1 = 0.6×230 + 0.4×3.5 = 139.4 GPa. Transverse and shear properties are lower, so plies are angled. A symmetric (mirror about the mid-plane), balanced (equal plus and minus angle plies) lay-up reduces coupling and warping; quasi-isotropic lay-ups spread plies over several directions so in-plane stiffness is similar in every direction.

sections.heading: Manufacturing and joining
sections.text: Metals are forged, cast, rolled and machined. Composites use hand lay-up, autoclave curing of pre-impregnated plies, resin infusion or resin transfer moulding. Process parameters must be controlled. Joining uses rivets, bolts, bonding and welding. Adhesive bonds spread load but need surface preparation. Riveted and bolted joints need hole quality and corrosion protection. Dissimilar metals, and carbon composites in contact with metals, can cause galvanic corrosion, so isolation is needed.

sections.heading: NDT and quality
sections.text: Non-destructive testing (NDT) finds defects without damaging parts. Visual inspection, dye penetrant, magnetic particle (ferromagnetic metals only), eddy current, ultrasonics and radiography are common. Quality control includes material traceability, process qualification, coupon tests (small test samples) and statistical checks. Approval rules for materials, processes and NDT personnel differ by country: FAA in the United States, EASA in Europe and NCAA in Nigeria set airworthiness requirements. Check current official sources.

keyPoints: Choose materials by specific strength and stiffness, temperature capability, fatigue, corrosion, cost and manufacturability.
Aluminium suits airframes, titanium hot airframe and engine parts, steel high-strength fittings, nickel superalloys hot engine sections, and composites weight-critical tailored structures.
Longitudinal lamina modulus is E1 = VfEf + VmEm; transverse and shear properties are lower.
Symmetric, balanced lay-ups reduce coupling and warping; quasi-isotropic lay-ups use several fibre directions for similar stiffness in all directions.
Joining by rivets, bolts, adhesive bonding or welding needs hole quality, surface preparation and galvanic corrosion control.
NDT methods include visual, dye penetrant, magnetic particle, eddy current, ultrasonic and radiographic testing; approval rules differ by country, so check the current authority.

en.title: Air-breathing propulsion: cycles and engines
en.short: Turbojet, turbofan, turboprop and ramjet cycles, components, thrust, fuel use and matching.

sections.heading: Engine types
sections.text: All air-breathing engines use atmospheric oxygen. A turbojet accelerates a small air mass to high speed. A turbofan adds a bypass stream driven by a fan; bypass ratio B is bypass mass flow divided by core mass flow. A turboprop uses a propeller and is efficient at lower flight speeds. A ramjet has no rotating compressor; forward speed raises pressure, so it needs a booster to start. Turbofans dominate airliners, turbojets and low-bypass turbofans suit high-speed military aircraft, and turboprops suit short regional flights.

sections.heading: Ideal cycle
sections.text: Ideal cycle analysis treats air as a perfect gas and the compressor and turbine as isentropic. For a turbojet, the Brayton cycle has pressure ratio r = p2/p1. Ideal thermal efficiency is η = 1 − 1/r^((γ−1)/γ). In an ideal turbojet, turbine work just balances compressor work; the nozzle then accelerates the exhaust to produce the jet. Example: γ = 1.4 and r = 10. Then r^0.2857 ≈ 1.931, so η = 1 − 1/1.931 ≈ 0.482, about 48%. Real efficiency is lower because of losses, and ram rise matters.

sections.heading: Real components
sections.text: Compressors raise pressure but stall or surge if pushed beyond their maps; multistage machines need bleed or variable stators. Combustors mix fuel and air, stabilise a flame, and limit emissions and temperature. Turbines extract work; inlet temperature is limited by blade material and cooling. Real cycle analysis adds component efficiencies, pressure losses and cooling. Specific fuel consumption (SFC) is fuel mass flow divided by thrust for jet engines; lower is better. Simple jet thrust is F ≈ m_dot(Vj − V0), with m_dot the mass flow.

sections.heading: Thrust and matching
sections.text: Bypass ratio trades jet velocity for mass flow: a high bypass turbofan gives high propulsive efficiency at moderate speed but a large nacelle. Engine and airframe matching means the engine’s thrust and SFC suit the aircraft’s mass, drag and mission. Example: m_dot = 50 kg/s, Vj = 600 m/s, V0 = 200 m/s. F = 50(600 − 200) = 20,000 N. With fuel flow 0.8 kg/s, SFC = 0.8/20,000 = 4 × 10⁻⁵ kg/(N·s), or 0.144 kg/(N·h).

keyPoints: Bypass ratio B = bypass mass flow ÷ core mass flow.
Ideal Brayton thermal efficiency is η = 1 − 1/r^((γ−1)/γ), where r is pressure ratio.
Simple jet thrust is F ≈ m_dot(Vj − V0), with a pressure term if the nozzle is not fully expanded.
SFC is fuel mass flow divided by thrust for jet engines; lower SFC means better fuel economy.
Compressor surge and turbine temperature limits are central real-cycle constraints.
Engine-airframe matching requires thrust and SFC to meet drag and mission at each flight condition.

en.title: Rocket propulsion
en.short: Rocket equation, thrust, specific impulse, nozzles, propellants, staging and electric propulsion.

sections.heading: Rocket equation
sections.text:
The ideal rocket equation gives velocity change Δv in free space with no gravity or drag: Δv = ve ln(m0 ÷ mf) = Isp g0 ln(m0 ÷ mf). ve is effective exhaust velocity, m0 and mf are masses before and after the burn, Isp is specific impulse, and g0 is standard gravity.

Example: ve = 3000 m/s, m0 = 10,000 kg, mf = 2,500 kg. The mass ratio is 4, ln 4 = 1.3863, so Δv = 3000 × 1.3863 = 4158.9 m/s, about 4.16 km/s. Real missions lose delta-v to gravity and drag.

sections.heading: Thrust and Isp
sections.text:
Thrust is the reaction to exhaust momentum. For nozzle exit area Ae, exit pressure pe and ambient pressure pa, F = mdot ve + (pe − pa)Ae, where mdot is propellant mass flow and ve here is the jet velocity at the nozzle exit. In vacuum pe > pa, so the pressure term adds thrust; at sea level pa may exceed pe, so it subtracts.

Specific impulse is Isp = F ÷ (mdot g0), usually in seconds. It measures thrust per unit weight flow. High Isp means less propellant for a given delta-v.

sections.heading: Nozzles and propellants
sections.text:
The nozzle converts thermal energy into a fast jet. Expansion ratio Ae ÷ At uses exit area Ae and throat area At. If pe < pa the nozzle is over-expanded; if pe > pa it is under-expanded. pa falls with altitude, so a fixed nozzle suits one altitude best.

Solid motors mix fuel and oxidiser in a grain. They are simple but hard to throttle or stop once lit. Liquid systems keep fuel and oxidiser in separate tanks. Pressure-fed systems use pressurant gas; turbopump systems use pumps driven by a turbine. Liquids allow throttling, shutdown and restart.

sections.heading: Staging and electric
sections.text:
Staging drops empty tanks and structure. Each stage follows the rocket equation; total delta-v is the sum of the stage delta-v values. Staging raises the mass ratio and so raises delta-v.

Electric propulsion uses electrical power to accelerate ions or plasma. It gives very high Isp but low thrust, so burns are long. A hybrid rocket has solid fuel and liquid or gaseous oxidiser; it can throttle and restart more easily than a solid motor.

keyPoints: Rocket equation: Δv = ve ln(m0 ÷ mf) = Isp g0 ln(m0 ÷ mf).
Thrust: F = mdot ve + (pe − pa)Ae.
Specific impulse: Isp = F ÷ (mdot g0), measured in seconds.
A nozzle is over-expanded when pe < pa and under-expanded when pe > pa.
Solid motors are simple but hard to throttle; liquid systems use pressure-fed or turbopump feed.
Staging raises delta-v; electric propulsion gives high Isp but low thrust.

en.title: Orbital mechanics
en.short: Two-body motion, Kepler’s laws, orbital elements, vis-viva, manoeuvres, transfers, perturbations and re-entry.

sections.heading: Two-body motion
sections.text: Two-body motion treats two point masses under mutual gravity. The relative acceleration is −μ r ÷ r³, where μ = GM is the gravitational parameter and r is the separation vector. Kepler’s laws say an elliptical orbit has the central body at one focus, sweeps equal areas in equal times, and has period T with T² = 4π²a³ ÷ μ, where a is the semi-major axis. The model ignores other bodies and non-spherical gravity.

sections.heading: Elements and energy
sections.text: Six orbital elements fix an orbit: semi-major axis a, eccentricity e, inclination i, right ascension of the ascending node Ω, argument of perigee ω and true anomaly ν. Specific orbital energy is ε = v² ÷ 2 − μ ÷ r = −μ ÷ (2a). The vis-viva relation follows: v² = μ(2 ÷ r − 1 ÷ a). A circular orbit has e = 0 and v = √(μ ÷ r); escape needs ε ≥ 0.

sections.heading: Manoeuvres
sections.text: The rocket equation gives a burn’s velocity change: Δv = ve ln(m0 ÷ mf) = Isp g0 ln(m0 ÷ mf), where ve is exhaust speed, Isp is specific impulse, g0 is standard gravity, and m0, mf are masses before and after. A Hohmann transfer uses two tangential burns between circular orbits; its transfer ellipse has a_t = (r1 + r2) ÷ 2. Example: r1 = 6,771 km, r2 = 42,164 km, μ = 398,600 km³/s². Then v1 = 7.672 km/s, v2 = 3.075 km/s, transfer speeds are 10.072 km/s and 1.617 km/s, so total Δv = 2.400 + 1.458 = 3.858 km/s. A plane change by Δi costs Δv = 2v sin(Δi ÷ 2) in a circular orbit.

sections.heading: Perturbations and entry
sections.text: Real orbits are perturbed. Atmospheric drag removes energy, lowering the orbit; Earth’s oblateness (the J2 term) makes the orbital plane precess. Launch combines a gravity turn with staging to limit gravity and drag losses. Re-entry converts kinetic and potential energy into heat, so vehicles use thermal protection and either ballistic or lifting entry.

keyPoints: Kepler’s third law: T² = 4π²a³ ÷ μ.
Vis-viva: v² = μ(2 ÷ r − 1 ÷ a), and specific energy ε = −μ ÷ (2a).
Rocket equation: Δv = ve ln(m0 ÷ mf) = Isp g0 ln(m0 ÷ mf).
A Hohmann transfer uses two tangential burns; a plane change by Δi costs Δv = 2v sin(Δi ÷ 2) in a circular orbit.
Drag lowers an orbit and Earth’s J2 oblateness causes precession of the orbital plane.
Launch losses and re-entry heating must be included in mission design.

en.title: Avionics and control systems
en.short: Feedback control, models, sensors, autopilots, fly-by-wire and integrated avionics.

sections.heading: Feedback control
sections.text: Feedback control compares a measured output with a command, forms an error and drives an actuator to reduce it. The controller might be proportional, integral or derivative action. Negative feedback reduces sensitivity to disturbances and plant changes, but too much gain causes oscillation or instability. Stability and margins are judged from the open-loop response.

sections.heading: Models and sensors
sections.text:
A transfer function G(s) is the Laplace-domain ratio of output to input for a linear system at rest. A state-space model uses first-order equations: xdot = Ax + Bu and y = Cx + Du, where x is the state vector. Sensors measure quantities such as rate, attitude, air data and position; actuators move surfaces or change thrust. Sensor errors and actuator limits affect the loop.

Example: G(s) = 9 ÷ (0.5s + 1) with unity feedback gives 9 ÷ (0.5s + 10) = 0.9 ÷ (0.05s + 1). A unit step settles to 0.9, with time constant 0.05 s.

sections.heading: Autopilots and fly-by-wire
sections.text: An autopilot is a control system that holds or follows a flight path. It usually has an outer guidance loop and inner attitude or rate loops. Flight control laws convert pilot or autopilot commands into surface and thrust commands, often with gains scheduled by airspeed and altitude. Fly-by-wire replaces mechanical linkages with electronic signalling and computers. Redundancy uses multiple channels, voting and dissimilar designs so one failure does not cause loss of control.

sections.heading: Integrated avionics
sections.text: Integrated avionics connects sensors, computers, displays and actuators through shared data buses. Integrated modular avionics shares computing resources among functions, which saves weight but needs careful partitioning. Certification rules for avionics differ by country and authority; check the current official source rather than assuming one country’s practice.

keyPoints: Negative feedback reduces error and sensitivity but can destabilise a loop if gain is too high.
A transfer function is G(s) = output(s) ÷ input(s) for a linear system at rest.
State-space form is xdot = Ax + Bu and y = Cx + Du.
For G(s) = K ÷ (τs + 1) with unity feedback, the closed-loop time constant is τ ÷ (1 + K) and the step steady value is K ÷ (1 + K).
Autopilots use outer guidance loops and inner attitude or rate loops; flight control laws map commands to surface and thrust actions.
Fly-by-wire needs redundancy, voting and dissimilar design; integrated avionics shares data buses and computing resources, and certification rules vary by country.

en.title: Aircraft systems
en.short: Hydraulic, pneumatic, electrical, fuel, ECS, ice protection and landing-gear architecture, redundancy and safety.

sections.heading: Architecture and redundancy
sections.text:
Aircraft systems are the functional groups that move, power, feed, cool and protect the aircraft. Architecture is how components are arranged and connected. Redundancy means providing more than one independent path so a single failure does not cause loss of a required function.

Certification authorities, such as the FAA in the United States and EASA in Europe, set safety requirements; these differ, so check the current rules. Requirements shape design: systems may be segregated, duplicated or made fail-safe. Fail-safe means a failure is evident and does not prevent continued safe flight. Dissimilar redundancy uses different technologies to avoid a common-mode failure, where one cause disables both paths.

sections.heading: Hydraulic and pneumatic
sections.text:
Hydraulic systems use a pressurised liquid to move actuators. Pascal’s law says pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted equally. Force equals pressure times piston area. Example: pressure 20 MPa on a piston area of 0.001 m² gives 20 × 10⁶ × 0.001 = 20,000 N.

Pneumatic systems use compressed air or gas for engine start, pressurisation and ice protection. They are lighter but less precise. Redundancy in both systems comes from multiple pumps or air sources, accumulators and separate circuits.

sections.heading: Electrical, fuel and ECS
sections.text:
Electrical systems generate, distribute and store power for aircraft loads. Multiple generators and essential buses provide redundancy. Fuel systems store fuel, feed the engines and manage the centre of gravity; cross-feed and multiple pumps allow a failed tank or pump to be isolated.

Environmental control systems (ECS) pressurise and condition cabin air, using bleed air or electric compressors. Fire zones and isolation valves limit fire spread.

sections.heading: Ice protection and gear
sections.text:
Ice protection is either anti-icing, which prevents ice forming, or de-icing, which removes ice. Methods include thermal systems using bleed air or electric heaters, chemical fluids and pneumatic boots.

Landing gear carries the aircraft on the ground, absorbs landing loads, and often retracts. Hydraulic actuation is common, with alternate extension for redundancy. Safety requirements shape these systems: they must tolerate failures. Rules differ by country, so check the current authority.

keyPoints: Aircraft systems are grouped by function and designed with redundancy so a single failure does not cause loss of a required function.
Hydraulic force equals pressure times piston area; for example, 20 MPa on 0.001 m² gives 20,000 N.
Redundancy can be parallel (duplicate) or dissimilar (different technology); the latter avoids common-mode failure.
Electrical systems use multiple generators and essential buses; fuel systems manage feed and centre of gravity.
Ice protection is anti-icing (prevent ice) or de-icing (remove ice); landing gear often has alternate extension.
Certification rules differ by country; check the current authority, such as the FAA in the United States or EASA in Europe.

en.title: Aircraft conceptual design project
en.short: Requirements, sizing, weight, layout, trade studies and certification review in aircraft design.

sections.heading: Requirements and constraints
sections.text: Conceptual design starts with a requirements document: payload, range, speed, field length, operating cost and safety targets. Each requirement becomes a constraint. Constraints may be physical (wing span, cabin size), operational (runway, noise) or regulatory. The design team states assumptions and margins explicitly, because a requirement missed late is expensive to fix.

sections.heading: Sizing and weights
sections.text:
Initial sizing estimates wing area S and thrust or power from wing loading W/S and thrust-to-weight T/W. Weight estimation uses a take-off weight budget: W0 = Wcrew + Wpayload + Wfuel + Wempty; for simple estimates crew may be lumped with payload. Empty and fuel fractions are first guessed from similar aircraft, then refined.

Example: if W0 = 50,000 N, payload plus crew = 10,000 N and fuel fraction is 0.25 of W0, then Wempty = 50,000 − 10,000 − 12,500 = 27,500 N. Check that the empty fraction 27,500 ÷ 50,000 = 0.55 is plausible for the class; if not, revise.

sections.heading: Layout and trade studies
sections.text: Configuration and layout place the wing, tail, engines, landing gear and payload. Trade studies compare options against weighted criteria such as mass, drag, cost and risk. Performance matching checks that the chosen wing loading and thrust-to-weight meet take-off, climb, cruise and landing requirements. A simple matching plot graphs W/S against T/W; the feasible region satisfies all constraints. Iterate until layout, weights and performance agree.

sections.heading: Review and certification
sections.text: Design review compares the evolving design with the certification basis. In the United States the FAA uses Title 14 CFR; in Europe EASA uses CS-23 or CS-25 for the aircraft category; Nigeria’s NCAA publishes its own regulations. Do not copy limits from memory: check the current official text. Professional registration also differs by country, for example COREN in Nigeria. Reviews record compliance methods, open risks and actions.

keyPoints: Conceptual design turns requirements into constraints and a baseline layout.
Initial sizing relates wing loading W/S and thrust-to-weight T/W to performance requirements.
Take-off weight budget: W0 = Wcrew + Wpayload + Wfuel + Wempty; fractions come from similar aircraft and are iterated.
Trade studies compare options against weighted criteria before detailed design.
Performance matching finds a feasible region of W/S and T/W that meets all mission constraints.
Design review checks compliance against the current certification requirements of the relevant country, such as FAA in the United States or EASA in Europe; professional registration rules also vary.

en.title: Space systems engineering: environment, budgets and assurance
en.short: Space environment, spacecraft subsystems and budgets, thermal, power, launch loads, ADCS, reliability.

sections.heading: Environment and budgets
sections.text: Spacecraft work in vacuum, with large temperature swings, radiation, atomic oxygen in low Earth orbit, micrometeoroids and debris. These drive design and testing. The bus carries the payload: structure, thermal, power, attitude determination and control (ADCS), data handling, communications and propulsion. Engineers track budgets for mass, power, data, thermal load and propellant. Each budget carries margin, an allowance for growth, and is reviewed as the design matures.

sections.heading: Thermal and power
sections.text: Thermal design balances heat in from the Sun, Earth and internal electronics against heat radiated to space. Multi-layer insulation, coatings, radiators, heat pipes and heaters keep units within limits. Thermal-vacuum tests check the model. Power design sizes solar arrays and batteries for sunlight and eclipse. Example: a 40 W payload and 20 W bus run continuously; a 60 W transmitter runs 20 minutes in each 100-minute orbit. Average load = 40 + 20 + 60 × (20 ÷ 100) = 72 W. A 35-minute eclipse needs 72 × 35 ÷ 60 = 42 Wh. At 80% depth of discharge (the fraction of capacity used), nominal capacity is at least 42 ÷ 0.8 = 52.5 Wh. Add margins for ageing and temperature.

sections.heading: Launch loads and structure
sections.text: During launch a spacecraft meets quasi-static acceleration, random vibration, acoustic noise and shock. The structure must be stiff enough to avoid harmful resonance and strong enough to survive these loads. Designers use the launcher user manual, which gives interface loads, frequency limits and factors of safety. These values differ by launcher and country, so use the current manual. Static and dynamic analysis plus vibration and acoustic tests show the structure and mounted units can withstand the launch environment.

sections.heading: Attitude, reliability, assurance
sections.text: ADCS determines attitude from sun sensors, star trackers and gyroscopes, then controls it with reaction wheels, thrusters or magnetorquers. Reliability is the probability of working without failure for a stated time. It is built in through redundancy, derating (running parts below their rated limits), failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA), qualification testing and configuration control. Mission assurance covers independent reviews, quality control and verification against requirements. Standards and processes differ between agencies and countries, for example NASA in the United States and ECSS in Europe; check current issue.

keyPoints: The space environment includes vacuum, thermal cycling, radiation, atomic oxygen and debris, so materials and tests must suit it.
Subsystem budgets for mass, power, data, thermal load and propellant need margins and regular review.
Average power is P_avg = Σ P_i × duty_i; battery energy is E = P_avg × t_eclipse and capacity is C = E ÷ DoD.
Thermal balance means heat absorbed from the Sun, Earth and electronics equals heat radiated to space.
Launch loads include quasi-static acceleration, vibration, acoustic noise and shock; use the current launcher user manual and its factors of safety.
ADCS uses sensors and actuators; reliability and mission assurance come from redundancy, derating, FMEA, qualification, reviews and configuration control.

en.title: Wind tunnel and flight testing
en.short: Similarity, tunnel types, corrections, instrumentation, flight tests and data reporting.

sections.heading: Similarity and scaling
sections.text:
Wind-tunnel tests use a scale model, so flow must be similar to full scale. Geometric similarity means the same shape at a different size. Dynamic similarity means the key dimensionless groups match, mainly Reynolds number Re = ρVL/μ = VL/ν and Mach number M = V/a, with ρ density, μ viscosity, ν = μ/ρ, V speed, L length and a sound speed. Matching both is often impossible.

Example: air with ν = 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s. A 0.3 m chord at 60 m/s gives Re = 60 × 0.3 ÷ (1.5 × 10⁻⁵) = 1.2 × 10⁶. A 3 m chord at 60 m/s gives 1.2 × 10⁷. Matching it with the small model needs 600 m/s, so pressurised or cryogenic tunnels help.

sections.heading: Tunnels and corrections
sections.text:
Tunnels are closed-circuit, recirculating air, or open-circuit, drawing fresh air. Test sections may be closed-wall or open-jet. They are also classed by speed: low-speed, transonic, supersonic and hypersonic.

Blockage is the reduction of test-section area by the model and wake, making local flow faster than the empty-tunnel value. Wall corrections adjust for walls constraining streamlines, changing lift, drag and pressure. Methods depend on tunnel and model, so use the calibrated method and check with different model sizes.

sections.heading: Instrumentation and data
sections.text: A strain-gauge balance measures forces and moments. Pressure taps with a scanner measure surface pressure. Hot-wire anemometry measures velocity, particle image velocimetry (PIV) maps flow, and schlieren shows density gradients. Data acquisition converts analogue signals to digital values. Set the sample rate above twice the highest frequency of interest, filter against aliasing, and calibrate every channel before a run.

sections.heading: Flight tests and reporting
sections.text: A flight-test plan defines objectives, safety limits and a test card listing speeds, altitudes and manoeuvres. Typical tests are level flight, climb, stall and control response. Telemetry and onboard recorders collect data. Analysis reduces data to coefficients, corrects to standard atmosphere, estimates uncertainty and compares with tunnel or computational results. The report states method, corrections, uncertainty and conclusions so the work can be repeated.

keyPoints: Dynamic similarity requires matching dimensionless groups, mainly Reynolds number Re = ρVL/μ = VL/ν and Mach number M = V/a.
A scale model usually cannot match full-scale Re and M together, so choose the dominant similarity and apply corrections.
Blockage and wall corrections account for the model and tunnel walls changing the flow; use the tunnel’s calibrated method.
Calibrate balances, pressure scanners and data channels, and sample above twice the highest frequency of interest to avoid aliasing.
A flight-test plan sets objectives, safety limits and a test card before data collection.
Report corrections, uncertainty and methods so results can be checked and repeated.

en.title: Computational methods: CFD and finite elements
en.short: Finite volume and finite element methods, meshing, boundary conditions, turbulence and validation.

sections.heading: Finite volume method
sections.text: The finite volume method (FVM) solves conservation laws for mass, momentum and energy. The domain is split into control volumes, and each equation is integrated over a volume. Fluxes through faces are balanced, so mass and momentum are conserved locally. Face fluxes are approximated from cell values, often with upwind or central schemes. A steady one-dimensional diffusion balance at an interior node with equal spacing gives T = (T_left + T_right) ÷ 2. FVM suits fluid flow and heat transfer.

sections.heading: Finite element method
sections.text:
The finite element method (FEM) divides a body into elements joined at nodes. Unknown fields are approximated by shape functions. Weighted residuals, often the Galerkin method, give element equations; assembly and boundary conditions yield Ku = F. For a two-node axial bar, k = EA ÷ L.

Example: a 2 m bar with EA = 2000 N is fixed at one end, loaded by 100 N at the other, and split into two 1 m elements. Assembly gives a displacement of 0.05 m at the mid node and 0.10 m at the loaded end, with the fixed end held at zero, matching FL ÷ EA = 100 × 2 ÷ 2000 = 0.10 m.

sections.heading: Meshes and boundaries
sections.text: Mesh generation turns CAD geometry into cells or elements. Quality matters: skewed or stretched cells increase error. CFD meshes often use thin boundary-layer cells near walls. Boundary conditions define the problem: inlet velocity or pressure, outlet pressure, no-slip walls and symmetry in CFD; fixed displacements, loads and supports in FEM. Wrong boundary conditions give plausible but wrong answers.

sections.heading: Turbulence and trust
sections.text: Most aerospace CFD does not resolve every turbulent eddy. Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) models time-averaged flow with eddy-viscosity models such as k-epsilon or k-omega SST. Large eddy simulation (LES) resolves large eddies and models small ones; direct numerical simulation (DNS) resolves all scales but is very costly. Verification checks the code and discretisation, for example by mesh refinement. Validation compares results with experiment. Certification uses validated methods and country-specific standards.

keyPoints: Finite volume methods integrate conservation laws over control volumes and balance fluxes, so mass and momentum are conserved locally.
Finite element methods approximate fields with shape functions; assembly gives Ku = F, and a two-node bar has k = EA ÷ L.
Mesh quality and correct boundary conditions are as important as the solver.
RANS models average turbulence with eddy-viscosity models; LES and DNS resolve more scales at higher cost.
Verification checks the numerical method; validation compares with experiment.
CFD and FEA support aerospace design, but results need validated methods and country-specific certification standards.

en.title: Airworthiness, maintenance and aviation safety
en.short: Type certification, continued airworthiness, maintenance, safety management and human factors.

sections.heading: Certification and continued airworthiness
sections.text: Airworthiness means an aircraft is safe for its intended flight. A type certificate approves the design of a type against the authority’s certification basis. The FAA does this in the United States, EASA in the European Union, and the NCAA (Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority) in Nigeria; ICAO sets international Standards and Recommended Practices (SARPs) but national rules differ. Each aircraft then gets an individual certificate of airworthiness. Continued airworthiness keeps it valid through maintenance, inspections, repairs, modifications and airworthiness directives, mandatory authority instructions.

sections.heading: Maintenance programmes and inspection
sections.text:
An operator’s maintenance programme sets scheduled tasks: checks at defined intervals, component overhauls, and inspections. MSG-3 (Maintenance Steering Group 3) is an industry decision process used to build programmes for large aircraft, but authorities approve the final programme. Inspection methods include visual checks, borescope, eddy-current and ultrasonic testing. Non-destructive testing finds cracks without damaging the component.

A small case: a Nigerian operator finds a crack in a landing-gear fitting during a scheduled check. The engineer grounds the aircraft, reports it through the required occurrence-reporting system, and the authority and manufacturer assess the fleet.

sections.heading: Safety management and accident models
sections.text: A safety management system (SMS) is a formal set of processes for managing risk. Under ICAO’s framework it has four parts: safety policy and objectives, safety risk management, safety assurance, and safety promotion. Accident models explain how failures combine. The Swiss cheese model (James Reason) pictures defences as slices with holes; an accident occurs when holes line up. The accident chain and SHEL model (software, hardware, environment, liveware) are also used. ICAO Annex 13 guides accident investigation; investigations aim to prevent recurrence, not to blame.

sections.heading: Human factors
sections.text: Human factors study how people work within systems. In maintenance, the Dirty Dozen lists common traps such as fatigue, complacency, distraction, pressure and poor communication. In flight operations, crew resource management trains pilots to use all available resources, and threat and error management trains crews to anticipate and recover from errors. Fatigue, automation and communication are central concerns. Regulators require reporting and just culture so that errors are learned from.

keyPoints: ICAO sets international SARPs, but national authorities such as the FAA, EASA and NCAA issue and enforce certificates.
A type certificate approves a design; a certificate of airworthiness approves an individual aircraft.
Continued airworthiness relies on approved maintenance, inspections and mandatory airworthiness directives.
An SMS has four components: policy, risk management, assurance and promotion.
Reason’s Swiss cheese model shows accidents occur when holes in defences align.
Human factors such as fatigue and communication are managed through CRM, TEM and reporting culture.

en.title: Professional practice, ethics and regulation
en.short: Ethics, national registration, sustainability, risk and the engineer’s duty to the public.

sections.heading: Ethics and codes
sections.text: A code of conduct sets the standards a profession expects. Common duties are competence, honesty, records, avoiding conflicts of interest, confidentiality and putting public safety first. In aerospace, a signed drawing or stress report may support a flight clearance, so false data can endanger lives. If pressed to approve unsafe work, refuse, record the concern and use the approved reporting route. Codes differ by institution and country; read the one that governs you.

sections.heading: Registration by country
sections.text: Registration is national or state-based. In Nigeria, COREN (the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria) registers engineers and regulates practice; check current requirements. In the United Kingdom, the Engineering Council maintains the national register and licenses professional institutions to assess titles such as Chartered Engineer (CEng). In the United States, a Professional Engineer (PE) licence is granted by each state board, usually after examinations and experience; no single national PE licence exists. A degree alone does not confer registration.

sections.heading: Sustainability and risk
sections.text: Sustainability means meeting present needs without unfairly limiting future generations. Aerospace engineers weigh fuel burn, emissions, noise, materials, maintenance and end-of-life recycling over the whole life cycle. Risk is the chance of harm and its severity. A simple risk score is likelihood × severity; compare it with your organisation’s matrix. ALARP (as low as reasonably practicable), used in UK safety regulation, asks whether further risk reduction is grossly disproportionate in cost. Record assumptions and residual risk.

sections.heading: Duty to the public
sections.text: The engineer’s first duty is to the public, ahead of employer or client. Sign only work you are competent to check, report test data honestly, and never hide a known defect.
